10754-little-sarah:
Little Sarah is a small picture book in verse for young children, from the "New Colored Toys" series. Sarah stands by her grandmother's bed and is sent to make a johnny-cake, mixed in one minute and baked in two. The meal barrel is empty, the shopkeeper has none, and Sarah must run to the miller to have corn ground in a minute.

The rhymes follow her errand step by step, with pictures to match, teaching patience and helpfulness through a simple task. The verse is plain and rhythmic, made to be read aloud. Families get a charming period nursery book, short enough for bedtime and easy for children to follow.
16503-another-world-fragments-from-the-s:
Writing as Hermes, the author of this 1873 book offers fragments from Montalluyah, a star city on another world. The preface cites Brewster and Proctor on the plurality of worlds, then promises an account of one star world's customs and moral state. Chapters treat Montalluyah itself, Vyora, perseverance, and the narrator's labors and triumph.

The book mixes utopian fancy with moral argument, asking whether men can be brought to seek knowledge as ardently as money. Its fragment form keeps the wonders brief and strange. Readers of early science fiction will find a curious Victorian vision of life beyond Earth.
20766-the-autobiography-of-methuselah:
A joke on damning the rain opens The Autobiography of Methuselah, from 1908. The teller weighs whether the wish means endless doom or a mere dam in the way. Such wordplay fits a life stretched across near a thousand years of Bible time.

John Kendrick Bangs, a famed humor writer, lends Methuselah his wit. The old man looks back on Adam, Noah, and a world grown young around him. Tall talk and gentle mockery fill the tale. Readers get a light, clever spin on the oldest man in scripture, told as if he wrote his own life at last.
21320-mass-george-a-boy-s-adventures-in-:
George Bruton, a young teenager on his father's Georgia plantation in the mid-eighteenth century, narrates George Manville Fenn's tale of the old Savannah. Captain Bruton, uneasy about slavery, buys an enslaved man and resolves to treat him well. The man's son joins the household, and the family nicknames him Pompey, or Pomp.

George and Pomp become fast friends through adventures with alligators, floods, fire, snakes, ants, and attacks by Native peoples and Spaniards from Florida. Much of the book is talk between the two boys. After the pair behave well through a long series of attacks, Captain Bruton decides to free both father and son.
21364-the-rajah-of-dah:
Ned, sixteen and fresh from school, begs to join his naturalist uncle's next expedition in George Manville Fenn's tale of Burma. They travel upriver past the trading port of Dindong to a British settlement under a British protectorate. The local ruler, the Rajah of Dah, proves an absurd and loathsome tyrant.

Ned and his English friend Frank catch an eighteen-foot crocodile among their adventures. Trouble sharpens when the Rajah sets his eye on a young British woman of the settlement for his harem. Fenn then turns the river journey into a rescue tale, with the settlement's quarrel with the Rajah coming to a head.
21485-the-young-rajah:
A young man sails to India in search of his father's papers in W. H. G. Kingston's The Young Rajah. The time is just before the Indian Mutiny, and unrest stirs across the land. His ship, the Glamorgan Castle, carries him to the Hooghly and a fateful meeting.

In the Rajah's territory, where his father once served, troubles break out around him. Slowly it emerges that the youth is the old Rajah's grandson and heir. The honour sits ill with him, since crowds treat him with awe. Shipboard love, a gallant rescue, and brisk action keep the tale moving well.
22663-a-ghetto-violet-from-christian-and:
Leopold Kompert wrote A Ghetto Violet, drawn from his novel Christian and Leah, a story of Jewish village life in Bohemia. The catalog record gives no year. Kompert was among the first writers to portray the ghetto from inside, with warmth and close knowledge of its customs.

In the sample, Ephraim refuses to sell or give away a caged bird, answering his sister's excitement with quiet calm. He would do nothing to pain her, he says, yet one word from him would make her open the cage herself and bid the bird fly home. The bird plainly stands for a human hope or bond. Kompert's gentle scenes preserve a world of faith, family pressure, and small freedoms that later history erased.
22749-from-edinburgh-to-india-burmah:
W. G. Burn Murdoch wrote From Edinburgh to India and Burmah, a travel narrative by the Scottish artist and explorer. The catalog record gives no year. Burn Murdoch sailed and sketched his way from Scotland to the East, and his book mixes voyage, pageantry, and the politics of empire.

The sample chapter deals with splendid royal shows in India. It even pauses for a curious dream: a prince and an aide-de-camp correct the abuses of the Royal Academies' privileges. Such whimsy sits beside durbar splendor and Burmese scenes in Burn Murdoch's manner. He writes as a painter talks: color first, commentary close behind. The book is a lively period record of the route from Edinburgh to Rangoon.
22843-aunt-deborah:
A hard family history stands behind Aunt Deborah, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. A clerk's son was driven from his father's door, tried, failed, and finally died broken-hearted. His widow, rosy-cheeked no longer, was driven off in her turn with her little boy. The old man kept his property close to the end.

When he died, within a year or two, he left everything to his daughter Deborah. That bequest makes Deborah the aunt of the title and the center of the tale. Mitford traces what money, grievance, and duty do inside one family across years. The story is sadder than her usual sketches. It shows her range, from comedy of manners into quiet tragedy.
23688-the-indulgence-of-negu-mah:
Robert Arthur published this science fiction story in Comet magazine in July 1941. Its hero is Negu Mah, a uranium merchant of Callisto. He sits in his garden under a shell of pure vitrite, sipping molkai with his guest Sliss, an amphibian from the swamps of Venus.

Negu Mah's wife Nanlo serves them as Jupiter rises over the horizon, and the slim shaft of the cargo rocket Vulcan stands ready, newest and swiftest of his freighter fleet. What begins as a leisurely visit among traders turns on the merchant's indulgence — a weakness, a wish, or a luxury that carries a price. Arthur tells it with color, humor, and a vivid sense of life across the solar system.
2478-the-circus-boys-on-the-plains-or-th:
Edgar B. P. Darlington sends his Circus Boys onto the plains as young advance agents, drumming up crowds for the show ahead of its arrival. The story follows the boys through prairie towns, where they post bills, dodge rivals, and learn the business side of the circus. The plains setting gives the adventure a western flavor.

The book's charm lies in its mix of showmanship and frontier travel. Young readers will enjoy the boys' growing responsibility. It stands as a sturdy middle volume of the series. Advance agents traveled ahead of the circus to plaster towns with posters.
30899-the-man-who-did-not-die-the-story-:
J. H. Willard wrote this retelling of the story of Elijah, published by Henry Altemus in Philadelphia in 1906 as part of Altemus' Beautiful Stories series, each volume selling for twenty-five cents. The series pairs it with The First Christmas, The First Easter, The Story of Solomon, The Story of Ruth, The Story of Elisha, and The Story of Samson. Willard tells the Bible story in plain, illustrated prose for young readers.

The book opens after the death of King Solomon, when his son Rehoboam becomes ruler of the Israelites. Heavy taxation to pay for Solomon's lavish court has left the people discontented and disloyal, and Rehoboam, following his younger counsellors, scornfully rejects their petition to lighten their burdens. Against that troubled kingdom, Elijah's story unfolds. It is a short, clear Bible tale, told for children.
3637-the-garden-of-allah:
Robert Hichens writes a romance set in Algeria, following Domini Enfilden to the desert town of Beni-Mora. The book is built in six parts: Prelude, The Voice of Prayer, The Garden, The Journey, The Revelation, and The Journey Back. Domini arrives after a rough sea journey, unable to sleep in the Hotel de la Mer, and wakes before dawn to catch her train inland.

In the Sahara she meets a mysterious stranger and falls in love, while the desert itself becomes a test of faith and desire. Hichens writes the landscape in rich, sensual prose, with gardens, prayer, and silence shaping the story. The novel suits readers who enjoy exotic romance and a heroine seeking God and love in the same journey.
3678-jonah:
Louis Stone writes an Australian novel about Jonah, a larrikin from Cardigan Street in Sydney. The story opens with a push gathered under a veranda, smoking and discussing horses and women, all young men from eighteen to twenty. Chapters follow Jonah eating green peas, discovering a baby, dealing it out with his mates, a quiet wedding, and Jonah starting on his own.

Later chapters take Jonah to Paddy's Market, to war with rivals, to the courting of Pinkey, and to the sign of the Silver Shoe, his own boot shop. Stone writes Sydney street life with humor and warmth, following a rough hero who builds a business and a family. The novel suits readers interested in Australian urban life before the First World War.
4246-beulah:
Augusta J. Evans set this novel in an orphan asylum, where the opening chapter finds a January sun shining on a large brick building surrounded by galleries and grounds. Beulah, the girl at its center, grows up among the asylum's inmates, under a matron's care, and the story follows her into young womanhood.

Evans, author of St. Elmo and Vashti, wrote Beulah as a novel of character and faith, in which an orphaned girl must find work, friendship, and a moral footing in the world. The long narrative moves from childhood scenes, church services, and small kindnesses toward the larger choices of adult life, with Southern settings and a strong religious thread.
4981-minnesota-and-dacotah:
C. C. Andrews's Minnesota and Dacotah gathers letters from a tour made in the autumn before publication, more than a hundred and thirty miles northwest of St. Paul. The author set out to satisfy himself about the character and prospects of the new territory, and wrote home what he found.

The letters, dedicated to the young men of Minnesota and published in 1857, describe land, settlement, and the chances open to newcomers. Andrews writes as an observer, not a promoter, noting both promise and hardship. Readers get a firsthand snapshot of the upper Mississippi frontier just before statehood changed it forever.
6869-the-american-goliah:
This pamphlet gives the only account its owners allowed of a stone figure found in Onondaga County, New York, on October 16, 1869. Shaped as a full grown man ten and one half feet tall, the figure was put forward as a petrified giant. The text gathers witness reports with the views of men of science on how such a body could turn to stone.

The publishers stress that every statement came from living witnesses on the spot, except where another source is named. They present the find as a wonder of the age and promise to add new tests, trials, and learned opinions as they arrive. The pamphlet itself serves as a running record of the Giant and its fame.
8016-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, hears that Jerusalem's walls lie in ruins and asks leave to rebuild them. The book that bears his name tells how he organised the work, wall by wall and gate by gate, despite mockery, threats, and plots from neighbouring peoples. It also records his reforms: debts forgiven, Sabbath kept, and the law read aloud to a weeping crowd gathered in the square.

Nehemiah is a book about rebuilding after ruin, and its hero is an organiser as much as a prophet. His prayers alternate with practical orders, giving the story unusual energy. In the King James Version, the first-person passages feel immediate, as if Nehemiah himself were reporting. The book has long encouraged readers facing the task of starting again.
8023-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Isaiah, the longest prophetic book, spans the crisis of Judah in the eighth century BC and looks far beyond it. The prophet denounces empty worship, corrupt rulers, and trust in foreign powers, warning that Assyria will punish the nation. Then, in passages of extraordinary poetry, he promises comfort: a suffering servant who bears the people's griefs, a new Jerusalem, and a peace in which swords become ploughshares. Both judgment and hope sound in the same voice.

Isaiah's influence is immense, in Jewish liturgy, in Handel's Messiah, and in Christian reading of the servant songs. Its images, the vineyard, the highway in the desert, the light to the nations, have shaped Western imagination. In the King James Version, the book's grandeur of language matches its scope, from court intrigue to the ends of the earth.
8024-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah of Anathoth, received God's word in the thirteenth year of King Josiah and kept prophesying through Jehoiakim and Zedekiah until Jerusalem was carried captive. His book is the longest in the Bible, mixing sermons, laments, symbolic acts, and personal confessions. He warns of Babylon's coming judgment, denounces false prophets who promise peace, and buys a field in besieged Jerusalem as a sign of future return.

Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet because his message cost him so much: prison, a cistern, and exile. Yet his promise of a new covenant, written on hearts rather than stone, became central to later faith. In the King James Version, his voice, tender and furious by turns, makes the book a profound study of a prophet who could not stay silent.
8038-the-bible-king-james-version-book-3:
Zechariah prophesied in Jerusalem in the second year of King Darius, after the exiles had returned from Babylon. His book opens with a call to turn back to God, unlike the fathers who ignored the former prophets. And then unfolds in a series of night visions: horsemen, horns, a measuring line, and a lampstand fed by olive trees. Later chapters promise a cleansed priesthood, a humble king riding on a donkey, and a restored city.

The visions are strange and vivid, and they encouraged a discouraged people to finish rebuilding the temple. Christians later read the humble king and the pierced one in these chapters as pointing to Jesus. In the King James Version, Zechariah's blend of warning and hope makes it one of the most imaginative books among the minor prophets.
8069-expositions-of-holy-scripture-isaia:
Alexander Maclaren's expositions on Isaiah, chapters one to forty-eight, and on Jeremiah work through the prophets sermon by sermon. His Isaiah titles include The Great Suit: Jehovah versus Judah, The Stupidity of Godlessness, What Sin Does to Men. The Perpetual Pillar of Cloud and Fire, A Prophet's Woes, Vision and Service, and The Kingdom and the King. Each exposition takes a passage and presses its meaning for the hearer's life.

Maclaren preaches the prophets as moral teachers, not distant oracles, and his commentary keeps the historical setting in view. The volume suits readers studying Isaiah and Jeremiah chapter by chapter, whether for preaching or private reading. It remains a respected example of Victorian expository preaching at its clearest.
8243-the-world-english-bible-web-nehemia:
Nehemiah was a Jewish official serving a Persian king when news reached him that Jerusalem lay in ruins. Its walls were broken and its gates burned, and the people who had returned from exile lived in shame and danger. With the king's leave, he traveled to Jerusalem and set about rebuilding the wall, facing mockery, threats, and plots from hostile neighbors.

The book mixes Nehemiah's own first-person account with lists of builders, gate by gate, and a public reading of the law that moved the people to tears. It is a story of grit, prayer, and practical leadership. Readers get both a vivid picture of life after exile and a portrait of a man who organized a broken city back into a community.
8250-the-world-english-bible-web-isaiah:
Isaiah, in the World English Bible, opens with the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Hear, heavens, and listen, earth, for Yahweh has spoken: he nourished children who rebelled against him. While the ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book moves from judgment to comfort.

The modern version keeps Isaiah's poetry direct, from the sinful nation loaded with iniquity to the promised servant and the new Jerusalem. Its plain sentences suit both study and reading aloud. For readers approaching the longest prophet, this rendering offers his grandeur without the barrier of Jacobean English.
8251-the-world-english-bible-web-jeremia:
Jeremiah was a prophet in Jerusalem during the last troubled decades of the kingdom of Judah, before Babylon destroyed the city. Called while still young, he warned kings and crowds alike that injustice, idol worship, and false confidence would end in disaster, and he was mocked, beaten, and imprisoned for it. His laments over his own people give the book its raw, personal edge.

The book mixes sermons, symbolic acts, letters to exiles, and confessions in which Jeremiah argues with God. It ends with the fall of Jerusalem, yet also promises a new covenant written on the heart. Readers meet a prophet who suffered for his message and still held that ruin was not the last word.
8260-the-world-english-bible-web-micah:
Micah, in the World English Bible, opens with the word of Yahweh that came to Micah the Morashtite in the days of Jotham. Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. Hear, you peoples, listen, earth, and let the Lord Yahweh be witness from his holy temple, for Yahweh comes forth. Treading the high places, while mountains melt like wax before fire and valleys split like waters poured down a steep place. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book denounces corruption and promises restoration.

The modern version keeps Micah's courtroom imagery sharp, including his famous call to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly. For readers of the minor prophets, this rendering gives a short, powerful book in clear contemporary language, moving from judgment to a hopeful remnant.
8265-the-world-english-bible-web-zechari:
Zechariah was a prophet among the Jews who had returned from exile to a ruined Jerusalem, and his book urges them to finish rebuilding the temple. The first half is a string of night visions: horsemen patrolling the earth, a measuring line stretched over the city, a lampstand fed by olive trees, and a flying scroll. Each vision pushes the tired builders back to work.

Later chapters speak in riddles about a humble king riding a donkey, a shepherd struck down, and a day when nations gather against Jerusalem and God intervenes. Christians have long read the humble king as pointing to Jesus. For any reader, Zechariah is a strange, vivid book where hope arrives in pictures rather than plain statements.
another-world-fragments-from-the-star-ci: Benjamin Lumley writes Another World, fragments from the star city of Montalluyah, published by Samuel Tinsley in London. The book imagines a society on another star, with its own customs, morals, and government, told through a visitor's fragments. Lumley's utopia joins Victorian speculation to a tale of wonder. Strange laws and rites fill the star city out.
beulah:
Augusta J. Evans's Beulah, her 1859 breakthrough novel, follows an orphan out of the asylum into a life she means to make her own. Beulah Benton is proud and clever: taken into the stern physician Guy Hartwell's household, she grows into a teacher and writer. Her real battle is inward. Reading philosophy and German skeptics, she argues herself out of the faith she was raised in, and finds the victory cold. Evans, not yet Augusta Evans Wilson, writes the South's most famous novel of religious doubt from inside the doubter.

The book made its young author famous on the eve of the Civil War. Its dialogues on faith fill drawing rooms as other novels fill ballrooms. Readers get the nineteenth-century woman's novel of ideas here: a heroine whose mind is the plot, and whose return to belief is argued, not assumed, page by hard page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allah:
Allah, the name of God in Arabic, compounds al and ilah, divinity, signifying the god par excellence. The form itself proves ilah was once an appellative, common to local and tribal gods. With the article it came to be restricted to one god who took precedence, and finally, with monotheism's triumph, was recognized as the only true God. The same root occurs in all Semitic languages for the Divinity.

Whether the name began as a proper name pointing to an early monotheism, later deviating into polytheism, is debated. It may instead have been an appellative that became a proper name only at monotheism. Before Mohammed's time the Arabs, through contact with Jews and Christians, were monotheists. Allah in Arabic theology matches God among Jews and Christians, except for the Trinity, which the Koran excludes. His attributes, denied by the Motazilites, number ninety-nine, each a bead of the Moslem chaplet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amrah:
In central Syria, where wood was scarce and the land often overrun by armies and brigands, builders learned to raise houses of stone alone. One such house at Amrah survives in fine condition. It stands round three sides of a courtyard, with a great hall rising two stories high. Its ground-floor bedrooms hold small canopied alcoves, and cupboards are cut from the thickness of the stone walls.

Houses of this Hauran kind sheltered the upper and middle classes from the third century to the seventh. Their stone craft explains why so many still stand. The Amrah house found a new life in modern times as the home of the sheikh of Douma. His household lives upstairs while business runs below, and the great hall keeps its ancient uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bettiah:
Bettiah, a Prefecture Apostolic in northern India, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Its jurisdiction includes the whole native state of Nepal, over 59,000 square miles with nearly three million people, bounded by Tibet, the Ghagra, the Ganges, and the Kusi. Capuchin missions opened the field.

In 1738 Father Joseph of Carignano, travelling toward Nepal and Tibet, stopped at Bettiah and cured the town's queen, who in return allowed him to preach. The Nepal war of 1769 and later troubles broke the mission's growth, but stations and schools survived. The entry is a frontier mission report on India's northern edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-nehem:
The Book of Nehemiah, also called the second Book of Esdras, tells how Jerusalem's walls rose again under Persian rule. Talmud and early Church counted it one book with Esdras, and Jerome still treated them together. Both were compiled and edited together, probably by the author of Paralipomenon about 300 before Christ. Nehemiah's own memoirs, however, justify reading it apart.

Its three sections open with Nehemiah, cup-bearer to Artaxerxes at Susa, hearing of Jerusalem's ruin in the king's twentieth year. His prudence wins him a mission with full powers to rebuild, lasting twelve years under the title Perah, or Athersatha. Earlier Jewish attempts under Xerxes and Artaxerxes I had stalled, and enemies had torn down part of the work. The middle section raises special literary problems and is treated last, after the wall narrative and the final chapter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delilah:
A scriptural entry examines Delilah, the woman of the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved after his exploit at Gaza. Sorek, known to Eusebius and Jerome and placed north of Eleutheropolis near Samson's home, is now Khan Sureq, on the borderland between Israelites and Philistines. Though Scripture never states her people, her dealings with Philistine princes make it unlikely she was an Israelite.

Nor is it likely she was Samson's wife: the text's phrasing, the Philistines' easy access to her house, and her readiness to betray him suggest a harlot, the common view among commentators. Believing Samson's strength came from a magical charm, the princes paid her to learn its secret. After false answers and mock bindings, her importunity won the truth: his Nazarite consecration and uncut hair. She had it shorn as he slept and handed him to his enemies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elijah:
Elijah, called Elias in this entry, was the loftiest prophet of the Old Testament, known chiefly from the narratives in the First Book of Kings. His Hebrew name means Yahveh is God. The stories, likely shaped in northern Israel near his own time, paint him in graphic detail. He is a desert man in a skin garment and leather girdle. He is swift of foot, at home in torrent beds and mountain caves.

He bursts onto the scene to tell King Ahab that God will punish Israel's apostasy with a long drought. Ahab, pushed by his Tyrian wife Jezebel, had built a Baal temple at Samaria, brought in foreign priests, and persecuted Yahveh's prophets. Of Elijah's birthplace nothing is sure, save that he was a Tishbite. The entry calls him a fire whose word burned like a torch. It follows his sudden comings and goings with the king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jonah:
Jonah is the fifth of the Minor Prophets, hero of the book that bears his name. His name usually means dove, but Jerome derived it from a root meaning to mourn, fitting his complaining words in chapter four. Outside his book he appears in 2 Kings, where Jeroboam II's recovery of Israel's borders fulfills the word spoken by Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-Hepher. Gath-Hepher was his probable birthplace, where his grave was shown in Jerome's day.

A tradition made him the son of the widow of Zarephath revived by Elijah, but the entry finds no basis for it beyond a play on names. The book's interest lies in two incidents: God's command to preach to Nineveh, Jonah's flight toward Tarshish, the storm, his confession, and his casting into the sea. They were followed by his reluctant preaching and Nineveh's repentance, which left the prophet complaining at God's mercy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-machpelah:
Machpelah is the burial ground by ancient Hebron that Abraham purchased from Ephron the Hittite for Sarah's grave. Sarah, Abraham, Rebecca, Leah, and lastly Jacob all rest in its cave, as Genesis records.

Hebrew usage, always with the article, makes Machpelah the field holding the cave, while Greek renders it the double cave, from kafal, to double, a sense taken into Targum, Syriac, and Vulgate. Josephus knows the tomb in the Hebron district. Rabbinic lore adds four patriarchs and even Adam, and Jerome carried that reading into the Vulgate. The Haram in south-east Hebron is identified with the tomb Josephus describes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massorah:
Massorah is the textual tradition of the Hebrew Bible, an official record of its words, consonants, vowels, and accents. The word may come from a verb meaning to hand down, seen in Ezekiel 20:37, or from a verb meaning to bind, since in the Mishna it chiefly means tradition. The main evidence for Massorah is the text itself in Hebrew Bible manuscripts, plus collections and marginal notes.

Jews treated sacred books as inspired code and record for national unity, so copyists from the first century B.C. trained to fix the text exactly, shunning novelty. Hebrew had no vowel letters, so certain consonants, matres lectionis, marked long vowels, and Sopherim, counters, counted every Torah letter. Later marginal notes marked Qere, read but not written, and Kethibh, written but not read. Seventeenth-century Protestants like the Buxtorfs called the text infallible, but modern critics treat it as one second-century witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-messiah:
Messiah, the Greek form Messias, transliterates the Hebrew for the anointed. The word appears only twice for the promised prince, in Daniel 9:26 and Psalm 2:2. Yet when a name was wanted for the promised one, at once King and Saviour, this royal synonym served naturally, marking both the King's dignity and his relation to God. The full title Anointed of Jahveh occurs in the Psalms of Solomon and the Apocalypse of Baruch, but the short form was in common use.

 In the Palestine Talmud the form with the article is nearly universal. The Babylonian Talmud's common use without the article is too weak an argument for antiquity to prove it a proper name in Christ's day. The entry proposes three tasks: outline the prophecies of the Messiah, trace their growth in later Judaism, and show how Christ vindicated his right to the title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-methuselah:
Methuselah, one of the Hebrew patriarchs named in Genesis 5, also appears as Mathusale and Mathusala. Scholars differ on his name's sense. Holzinger offers man of the javelin. Hommel and many others offer man of Selah, Selah being a Babylonian word and title of the god Sin. Sayce traces it to a Babylonian word not understood. Genesis traces his descent through his father Henoch to Seth, a son of Adam and Eve.

 When Methuselah reached one hundred and eighty-seven he became father of Lamech, then lived seven hundred and eighty-two more years, dying at nine hundred and sixty-nine. His death thus fell in the year of the Deluge. No other human is recorded to have lived so long, so Methuselah has become a byword for longevity. Rationalists and advanced critics deny the patriarchs' great ages outright, while Catholic commentators accept Genesis's words without difficulty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-olah:
Hungarian primate Nicolaus Olah, born at Nagyszeben in 1493, rebuilt church life in a kingdom torn by Turks and reformers. Page at the court of Wladislaw II, then secretary to kings and to Queen Mary, he followed her to the Netherlands in 1531 and stayed a decade.

Back in Hungary in 1542, Olah rose from royal chancellor and bishop of Agram to archbishop of Esztergom in 1553. He crowned kings, founded schools and a seminary, pressed for a learned clergy, and left letters and notes that light up his age. He died in 1568. His autobiographical notes and letters show his crowded career in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-noah:
Noah, ninth patriarch of the Sethite line and son of Lamech, stands in Genesis as the second father of humankind. His name, tied to rest and comfort, answered his father's hope that the boy would ease the curse laid on the ground after Adam.

Amid a corrupt age, Noah walked with God, built the Ark at divine command, and carried his family and the animals through the Flood. Afterward he planted a vineyard, and the entry weighs his drunkenness, his blessing and curse on his sons, and his 950 years. Commentators read Lamech’s words as hope, prophecy, or a father’s wish for rest in old age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savannah:
Savannah, a diocese covering the state of Georgia, was created by Pius IX in 1850. Its first bishop, Francis Xavier Gartland of Philadelphia, was consecrated on 10 September 1850 and died four years later. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lists a quick succession of bishops in a young southern see.

John Barry of Augusta followed in 1857 and died in 1859. Augustus Verot, vicar apostolic of Florida, succeeded but resigned in 1870 and returned to Florida, dying in 1876. Ignatius Persico, transferred from Charleston in 1870, resigned two years later through ill health. William Gross, consecrated in 1873, moved to Oregon City in 1885, and Thomas Becker, transferred from Wilmington in 1886, died in 1899. Bernard Keiley then took charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophonias-zep:
Sophonias, better known as Zephaniah, was the ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets, preaching in Jerusalem in the second half of the seventh century before Christ. A contemporary and supporter of Jeremiah, he takes his name from a Hebrew word meaning the Lord conceals, or the Lord protects. And his whole surviving work runs to only three short chapters.

His ministry fell under King Josias, after the idolatrous reigns of Amon and Manasse had filled Jerusalem with the cults of Baal and Astarte. The entry draws everything known about him from that brief book, tracing its warnings, its hopes, and its place in the reform that Josias would soon attempt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-torah:
Torah first means direction or instruction, as a parent's teaching or a wise man's counsel, and chiefly God's instruction through Moses and the prophets. In the sense of law it means only divine laws. The word also names the books holding the Mosaic revelation and law, that is, the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible.

In Jewish theology Torah can mean the whole body of Jewish doctrine, whether as a guide for belief and conduct or as a field of study. It can also mean the entire Scriptures, or single passages from Prophets and Writings. The entry then details the Pentateuch itself. It counts 290 open and 379 closed paragraphs, Sabbath lessons on a three-year cycle in Palestine, and 154 to 175 sedarim, or reading sections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urmiah:
Urmiah is a residential see in Chaldea, in the Persian province of Adherbaidjan. Its primitive name seems to have been Urmui, or rather Urmedji. It is said, but with little truth, to be the birthplace of Zoroaster, who supposedly lived in a nearby grotto. Nothing is known of its early history. Some wrongly place at Urmiah Bishop John of Persa, present at Nicaea in 325.

The Synodicon of the Chaldean Church makes no mention of Urmiah for several centuries. On the other hand a See of Adherbaidjan existed from 420 to the thirteenth century, suffragan of Arbela. Yet no proof shows its bishop lived at Urmiah rather than elsewhere in the province. The entry sorts these claims with care, leaving Urmiah's early church history largely open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-utah:
Utah, the thirty-second state admitted to the Union, takes its name from the Ute or Yuta tribe, a Shoshonean people whose hunting grounds covered three-fourths of the state. It measures 350 miles long and 275 miles wide, with an area of 84,990 square miles, of which 2,780 are water. The thirteenth census counted 373,351 people. Nevada bounds it west, Colorado and Wyoming east, Arizona south, and Idaho and Wyoming north.

The Wasatch and Uintah ranges cross the state from north to south, with lesser heights giving variety to basins and valleys. The entry describes its physiography, climate, resources, and people, then turns to church history: the Mormon settlement, the coming of Catholic missionaries, and the diocese's parishes and schools. It offers a full state portrait with a Catholic focus.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-isaiah-and:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on Isaiah and Jeremiah gathers sermons on the two great prophets. Alexander Maclaren expounds Isaiah chapters I to XLVIII in the first part. Jeremiah follows in the same sermon form. Each entry grows from a brief quoted text.

Isaiah entries open with The Great Suit: Jehovah versus Judah. Vision and Service treats the prophet's call in chapter VI. The Kingdom and the King takes up the child of Isaiah IX. Later pieces include The Song of Two Cities and Light or Fire. Maclaren often pairs a striking image with a moral turn. His titles, such as The Sucker from the Felled Oak, show that habit. The volume serves preachers and lay readers alike.
jonah:
Jonah is a novel by Louis Stone about a Sydney larrikin, not the biblical prophet. Its contents divide into two parts, Larrikins All and The Sign of the Silver Shoe. Jonah's world is Cardigan Street, street corners on Saturday night, and the Push, his gang. Early chapters show him eating green peas, discovering a baby, and courting Pinkey.

A quiet wedding follows, and Jonah starts out on his own at Paddy's Market. The second part centers on the Silver Shoe, a family in exile, and Mrs. Partridge lending a hand. Death, a two-up school, and a fatal accident darken the later chapters. Stone writes the rough humor and hard luck of working-class Sydney life in Jonah's story.
little-sarah:
An unknown maker shaped this colored toy book in verse. Little Sarah stands by her grandmother's bed at breakfast time. Grandmother wants a Johnny-cake mixed in one minute flat. It must bake in two minutes more, grandmother insists.

The meal barrel stands empty as wind, Sarah discovers. The shopkeeper sends her running to the miller instead. The miller sends her onward to the cornfield over the hill. Each errand repeats the hurry of the cumulative rhyme. The corn had not grown when Sarah reached the field. Her chain of errands stretches the Johnny-cake's two minutes delightfully.
minnesota-and-dacotah:
C. C. Andrews wrote these letters after touring the Northwest in the autumn of 1856. He was a counselor at law and editor of the official opinions of the attorneys general. The second edition appeared at Washington in 1857. His title page quotes Longfellow's lines about the land of the Ojibways and the Dacotahs.

Andrews describes Minnesota and the Dacotah country for eastern readers. He adds information about public lands and a table of statistics. Such books guided emigrants choosing where to settle in the territories. His letters preserve a lawyer's careful view of the upper Mississippi country just before Minnesota statehood.
tanakh-jps-1917-isaiah:
Isaiah is the longest prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English Bible. It is called the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz, seen in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

Heaven and earth are called to hear a sharp charge: children raised by God have turned away in revolt. Ox and ass know their masters, yet Israel does not know its maker. The land lies waste, towns burn, and Zion sits lone as a booth in a vineyard. Readers get grand verse that swings from blame and ruin to comfort and hope, long prized as the peak of Hebrew prophecy.
tanakh-jps-1917-jeremiah:
Jeremiah is a long prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the Masoretic-based English of the Jewish Publication Society from 1917. Jeremiah is named as son of Hilkiah, of the priests at Anathoth in Benjamin.

His call comes in the thirteenth year of King Josiah and runs through the fall of Jerusalem under Zedekiah. The young man pleads that he is a mere child who cannot speak, but God touches his mouth and sets him over nations. Readers follow a lone voice through siege, grief, and blame, tasked to root out and pull down, yet also to build and to plant.
tanakh-jps-1917-jonah:
Jonah is a short story book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the 1917 English of the Jewish Publication Society. Jonah son of Amittai is told to go to Nineveh, the great city, and speak out against it.

Rather than obey, Jonah flees by ship, and a great storm rises that threatens to break the vessel apart. The crew cast lots, the lot falls on Jonah, and he tells them to throw him into the sea. Once they do, the sea grows calm, and a great fish swallows him for three days and nights. Readers meet a runaway prophet whose brief tale probes mercy shown even to a foe city.
tanakh-jps-1917-micah:
Micah is a short prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the 1917 English Bible of the Jewish Publication Society. Micah the Morashtite speaks in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, with words about Samaria and Jerusalem.

All peoples are called to hear as God comes down and treads the high places, melting hills like wax. The cause is the sin of Jacob, pinned on Samaria's idols and Jerusalem's high places alike. Micah warns that carved images will be smashed and the city made a heap. Readers meet bold verse that blasts rich abuse of the poor, yet also holds a famed hope for peace among nations.
tanakh-jps-1917-nehemiah:
Nehemiah is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society version of the Holy Scriptures. Nehemiah serves as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia when word of Jerusalem's ruin reaches him.

He prays in grief for his people's sins, then waits for a chance to speak to the king. In the month Nisan, the king notes his sad face and asks what he needs. Nehemiah asks to be sent to Judah to rebuild the city of his fathers' tombs, and gains royal letters and timber. Readers follow wall building under threat, debt relief, and a renewed pledge to the law in a small, weak province.
tanakh-jps-1917-obadiah:
Obadiah is the shortest book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society English of 1917. It is called the vision of Obadiah, and its whole word is aimed at Edom, Israel's old foe and kin.

A report from God has been heard, and a herald sent among the nations to rise up against Edom in war. Edom is charged with pride in its rock strongholds and with standing aloof when Jerusalem fell. The book warns that as Edom has done, so it shall be done in return. Readers get one sharp chapter of judgment, paired with a close that gives Mount Zion to those who escape and the kingdom to God.
tanakh-jps-1917-zechariah:
Zechariah is a long book among the short prophets, presented in the Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917. Zechariah son of Berechiah is placed in the second year of Darius, king of Persia, after the return from exile.

God tells the people that he was sore displeased with their fathers, who shut their ears to past prophets. He calls this new age group to turn back to him so that he will turn back to them. Soon Zechariah sees a night vision of a man among trees. Readers get strange visions of horses, horns, and a flying scroll, plus clear calls to rebuild the temple and live justly.
tanakh-jps-1917-zephaniah:
Zephaniah is a short prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society rendering of 1917. Zephaniah son of Cushi speaks in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.

His word is stark: God will sweep all things from the face of the earth, man and beast, birds and fish alike. Judah and Jerusalem face the cut for Baal worship, roof-top star rites, and mixed oaths sworn to two gods at once. Readers get a grim day-of-the-Lord warning in three short chapters, which still ends with song, as God is said to rejoice over a cleansed and gathered people.
the-american-goliah:
A pamphlet from 1869, billed as the only authorized account from the owners, tells of a stone giant dug up in Onondaga County, New York. The find, dated October 16, 1869, is said to be a perfectly formed man ten and one-half feet high. Its sellers, Redington and Howe, promise fresh facts and expert views as they appear.

Boosters call the stone figure perhaps the greatest find of the century in this country. The pages gather witness statements taken on the spot, press reports, and the views of learned men on the supposed petrified body. Cuts showing points of interest were still being prepared when this early issue went out.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-16-neh:
Nehemiah , read in the King James Version, begins with the words of Nehemiah, son of Hachaliah, at Shushan the palace in the month Chisleu, in a twentieth year. Hanani, one of his brethren, arrives with men from Judah.

Nehemiah asks about the Jews left from captivity and about Jerusalem. The answer is grim: the remnant is in great affliction and reproach, the wall is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire. Hearing it, Nehemiah sits, weeps, mourns for days, fasts, and prays. His prayer confesses Israel's sins as well as his father's house.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-23-isa:
Isaiah , given here in King James English, opens with a vision of Isaiah, son of Amoz, concerning Judah and Jerusalem. It is dated to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

Heavens and earth are called to hear, for God says he raised children who rebelled. An ox knows its owner and an ass its master's crib, but Israel does not consider. The nation is called sinful, laden with iniquity, and sick from head to foot, with wounds and sores. Charge and lament open a long prophetic book aimed at a people who have forsaken their God.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-24-jer:
Jeremiah in the authorised King James wording, opens with the words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, from the priests at Anathoth in Benjamin. God's word came to him in the thirteenth year of Josiah and continued through Jehoiakim to Zedekiah's eleventh year, when Jerusalem was carried captive.

Before I formed thee I knew thee, God tells him, ordaining him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah protests that he is a child who cannot speak. God answers that he must go where sent and say what is commanded. Calling, fear, and a long span ending in exile frame the book.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-38-zec:
Zechariah in the King James text, starts in the eighth month of Darius's second year. The word comes to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo the prophet.

God has been sore displeased with your fathers, the message begins. Turn to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will turn to you. Do not be like the fathers, who heard former prophets cry for a turn from evil ways and would not listen. Where are those fathers now, Zechariah asks, and do prophets live forever? Return after exile, urged through a dead generation's failure, opens the book.
the-circus-boys-on-the-plains-or-the-you: The Young Advance Agents Ahead of the Show is the subtitle Edgar B. P. Darlington gave this Circus Boys tale of work on the plains. Greg Berckes prepared the Gutenberg text, released in January 2001 as etext 2478. A standard Gutenberg header fills the whole of what is present. No advance-agent chapter follows it, so the boys' work ahead of the show goes undescribed here.
the-garden-of-allah:
Robert Hichens wrote The Garden of Allah as a novel of the Algerian desert, first printed in 1904. Three books divide the tale: a prelude, the voice of prayer, and the garden itself.

Hichens sets a disgraced monk and a young English woman on a path through the sands, where faith lost and found drives each scene. The desert works on both like a vast church, stripping wealth and rank to bare soul. The book made Hichens famed in his day for lush scenes of sand, palms, and prayer, and for a love tale crossed by vows no priest can loose.
the-world-english-bible-web-isaiah:
Book twenty-three in the World English Bible presents the vision of Isaiah, son of Amoz. He prophesies about Judah and Jerusalem under four kings. Heaven and earth are summoned to listen. God says he raised children who rebelled against him. Even an ox knows its owner, Isaiah laments. Israel, by contrast, does not consider its master.

The nation is called sinful and loaded with iniquity. Its whole head is sick, its heart faint. Wounds and open sores cover it, the prophet says. Why invite more beating by revolting further, he asks. Judgment opens the book, yet promises of restoration follow. Isaiah shapes later faith with unmatched poetic power.
the-world-english-bible-web-jeremiah:
Jeremiah's words form book twenty-four in the World English Bible. He is Hilkiah's son, from a priestly family in Anathoth. God's word first came to him under King Josiah. His ministry ran through Jehoiakim's reign to Zedekiah's end. It closed when Jerusalem was carried away captive. Jeremiah then recalls his call as a young man.

God says he knew Jeremiah before forming him in the womb. He was appointed a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah protests that he is only a child who cannot speak. God rejects the excuse and sends him anyway. Readers follow a reluctant prophet through decades of unwelcome warnings.
the-world-english-bible-web-micah:
Micah speaks in book thirty-three of the World English Bible, a prophet from Moresheth. His word comes under kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Samaria and Jerusalem both fall under his gaze. All peoples are told to hear his warning. God himself will witness against them from his temple. He comes down and treads the earth's high places.

Mountains melt under him like wax before fire. Valleys split like water poured down a slope. Jacob's disobedience, Micah says, causes this judgment. Samaria will become a rubble heap in the field. Later chapters promise a ruler from Bethlehem. Readers hear fierce justice joined with surprising hope for the humble.
the-world-english-bible-web-nehemiah:
Book sixteen in the World English Bible gives the words of Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah. He is at the palace in Shushan during the month Chislev. His brother Hanani arrives with men from Judah. Nehemiah asks about Jews who survived the captivity. Their report is grim: the remnant suffers great affliction. Jerusalem's wall lies broken and its gates burned.

Hearing this, Nehemiah sits down and weeps. He mourns for days, fasting and praying. His prayer calls God great and awesome. Covenant mercy for those who love God anchors his plea. A cupbearer will soon rebuild a city. Readers watch prayer turn into organized, risky action.
the-world-english-bible-web-zechariah:
Zechariah prophesies in book thirty-eight of the World English Bible, during Darius' second year. He is Berechiah's son and Iddo's grandson. God's opening word recalls anger at Israel's fathers. Earlier prophets urged repentance, but the fathers would not listen. Now God calls the new generation back to him. He promises to come back to them in turn.

The fathers are gone, Zechariah notes, and prophets do not live forever. God's words, though, overtook that older generation. Night visions of horsemen, horns, and a flying scroll follow. A restored Jerusalem and a coming king fill later chapters. Post-exile hope takes strange, vivid shapes here.
